When Parameter Gradient Flows Close in Representation Space

Shengye Tao Affiliation: Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications (BIMSA) Affiliation: Beijing, China Email: ShengyeTao@bimsa.cn    RanchoTao@gmail.com
October 20, 2026
Abstract

The represented gradient flow of a parameterized model depends on a mobility that can retain hidden parameter information. We study when one entire represented mobility map works for every autonomous loss from one fixed initialization. For two-factor matrix representations wider than both output dimensions, with individually full-row-rank factors, we classify all admissible joint ranks: closure occurs precisely at effective scalar-balanced minimal joint rank or a two-value signed spectral family at full joint rank. All intermediate ranks are excluded; positive represented flows belong to known square-root families. For general representations with constant ambient representation and gradient-Lie ranks, ordinary closure is equivalent to a local invariant-level metric in the analytic case and specified smooth regimes. An endpoint section forces the initially unrestricted mobility map to admit a locally smooth representative on the represented image. We also separate testing families: linear losses locally admit closure at every submersion, whereas one fixed translated strongly convex quadratic family fails it on a delayed-bracket example. A fixed output readout gives an ordinary squared-loss witness. These supporting results do not characterize quadratic-only closure in general. We retain the unresolved smooth output-rank-two case with Lie rank at least four. A frozen deterministic experiment checks a separate engineered-loss construction; it is distinguished from the squared-loss proof, universal theorems and empirical learning performance.

1 Introduction

For an open parameter domain Ω⊂ℝD\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{D} and a smooth representation ϕ:Ω→ℝd\phi:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, parameter gradient flow of a represented loss ff gives

θ˙=−D​ϕ​(θ)T​grad⁡f⁡(ϕ⁡(θ)),z˙=−M⁡(θ)​grad⁡f⁡(z),M=D​ϕ​D​ϕT.\dot{\theta}=-D\phi(\theta)^{T}\grad f(\phi(\theta)),\qquad\dot{z}=-M(\theta)\grad f(z),\qquad M=D\phi D\phi^{T}. (1)

States with the same zz may have different MM. We ask when the entire mobility, rather than only its action on the gradient of a particular loss, is determined by zz along all loss trajectories from one fixed initialization. This is the ordinary intrinsic-dynamic contract of [1], distinct from its stronger piecewise-loss testing convention.

The two results proved below are an initialization classification for wide two-factor matrix representations and a converse from ordinary trajectory tests to invariant-level metric factorization for regular representations in stated analytic and smooth regimes. All positive matrix mobilities reduce to known scalar-balanced flows; no new optimizer, optimization rate or task gain is claimed. The distinction is a necessity theory for eliminating hidden mobility, not a new formula for the already known positive flow. The loss-family quantifier is substantive: Proposition 6.1 shows that all linear tests can pass locally at a submersion, while Theorem 6.3 and Corollary 6.4 give exact nonclosure with familiar output least-squares losses in a fixed model. The latter are supporting exclusion controls, not new learning algorithms. Generic continuous initializations in the nonscalar wide model fail this exact closure, as a direct consequence of the classification. This does not exclude approximate closure or a simpler description under one particular loss.

The work uses the conservation-law and Lie-distribution framework of [2, 1]. In particular the gradient Lie algebra and maximal-stack factor-orbit dimensions in the matrix proof are prior ingredients, explicitly attributed below. The additional inference under study is how single-initialization, autonomous-loss tests constrain Gram fibers and a local invariant-level mobility. Familiar Frobenius, constant-rank, inverse-function, orbit and ODE results are used as standard local theorems, with their hypotheses identified at each application.

Results and reading guide.

Theorem 3.1 gives an initialization classification, including the distinction between minimal, intermediate, and full joint rank. Theorem 4.2 supplies the fixed-start converse in its stated regular regimes. Theorem 6.3 separates linear testing from a fixed-Hessian quadratic family; Corollary 6.4 transfers the witness to squared error after one fixed readout. The scalar-output case and positive square-root flows are known. Section 7 compares these statements with specific predecessor results. Complete proofs are in the appendices.

2 Problem Setting and Definitions

Fix θ0∈Ω\theta_{0}\in\Omega. A solution on an open set means its forward maximal local interval before exiting that set; no global-time existence is assumed. Losses are global 𝒞2\mathcal{C}^{2} maps f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} without a common bound on their derivatives. Neighborhoods can depend on initialization but not on the tested loss.

Definition 2.1 (Ordinary entire-mobility closure).

Property (O) holds at θ0\theta_{0} if there exist an open neighborhood U∋θ0U\ni\theta_{0} and a single map K:ℝd→ℝd×dK:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} such that every solution of (1) from θ0\theta_{0}, for every global 𝒞2\mathcal{C}^{2} loss, satisfies M⁡(θ⁡(t))=K⁡(ϕ⁡(θ⁡(t)))M(\theta(t))=K(\phi(\theta(t))) on its interval in UU. The map KK is independent of the loss and is initially unrestricted: continuity, boundedness and differentiability are not assumptions.

Definition 2.2 (Local invariant-level metric).

Property (I) holds if, on a parameter neighborhood, there are finitely many common 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} conservation laws h=(h1,…,hk)h=(h_{1},\ldots,h_{k}) and one globally 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} map K¯:ℝd→ℝd×d\overline{K}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} such that

M(θ)=K¯(ϕ(θ))for every θ∈V∩{h=h(θ0)}M(\theta)=\overline{K}(\phi(\theta))\quad\hbox{for every }\theta\in V\cap\{h=h(\theta_{0})\}

for some open V∋θ0V\ni\theta_{0}. Common conservation means D​ϕ​grad⁡hj=0D\phi\,\grad h_{j}=0 on the domain of hh.

The laws hh are local, as in the conservation-law convention of [1]; the represented extension K¯\overline{K} is global. Equality is required on the actual local level, not merely on its tangent. Conservation and substitution immediately give (I)⇒\Rightarrow(O). The strong intrinsic dynamic property of [1, Definition I.2] instead tests piecewise 𝒞2\mathcal{C}^{2} represented losses ff, requiring a continuous trajectory from θ0\theta_{0} to follow −∇(f∘ϕ)-\nabla(f\circ\phi) wherever ff is differentiable along its represented path, with one common neighborhood and one common KK. This is a spatial piecewise-loss convention; arbitrary time-dependent switching is a separate testing class. Strong closure implies ordinary closure, so an obstruction to strong closure alone does not prove failure of ordinary closure. Finite flow concatenations below are auxiliary geometric constructions; each ordinary witness is realized by an actual smooth autonomous loss from the fixed initial state.

No positive definiteness on all target space is part of these definitions: the mobility may be semidefinite when the representation rank is less than dd.

Let Xi=grad⁡ϕiX_{i}=\grad\phi_{i} and let EθE_{\theta} be the span of the values at θ\theta of their generated Lie algebra. We use the bracket [X,Y]=D​Y​X−D​X​Y[X,Y]=DY\,X-DX\,Y. When dimE=p\dim E=p is constant on an ambient neighborhood, selecting a nonzero minor of finitely many bracket fields gives a smooth frame for EE. The frame brackets lie in EE, so Frobenius applies. It supplies a local product box with common first integrals hh and a connected initial plaque L={h=h(θ0)}L=\{h=h(\theta_{0})\} of dimension pp. If p=Dp=D, take hh constant. If rank⁡D​ϕ=q\rank D\phi=q is constant as well, then

rank⁡D⁡(ϕ|L)=q≤p,\rank D(\phi|_{L})=q\leq p, (2)

because im⁡D​ϕT⊂T​L\operatorname{im}D\phi^{T}\subset TL and im⁡(D​ϕ​D​ϕT)=im⁡D​ϕ\operatorname{im}(D\phi D\phi^{T})=\operatorname{im}D\phi. The analytic versions follow by selecting analytic frames and using analytic Frobenius. These statements concern one local plaque and require neither globally embedded leaves nor a global quotient.

Lemma 2.3 (Compatible loss on an embedded represented arc).

Let a smooth parameter curve satisfy θ˙=−D​ϕ​(θ)T​g​(t)\dot{\theta}=-D\phi(\theta)^{T}g(t) with smooth gg, and suppose its represented curve γ=ϕ∘θ\gamma=\phi\circ\theta is a regular embedded compact arc admitting a slightly extended embedded arc. Then this curve is a trajectory of one global smooth autonomous represented loss from its given initial point.

Proof. See Appendix A.1.

Lemma 2.4 (Clock-positive endpoint patch).

Suppose a local embedded manifold L∋θ0L\ni\theta_{0} is invariant for all fields Yg=−D​ϕT​gY_{g}=-D\phi^{T}g, g∈ℝdg\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and their Lie values span Tθ​LT_{\theta}L on LL. Assume M⁡(θ0)≠0M(\theta_{0})\neq 0. Every sufficiently small ambient neighborhood admits a nonempty LL-open set of endpoints from θ0\theta_{0}, each realized by one global smooth autonomous represented loss with its whole path in that neighborhood. Consequently (O) implies M=K∘ϕM=K\circ\phi on this set. Constant Lie rank in the ambient parameter space is not required.

Proof. See Appendix A.2.

Lemma 2.5 (Linear losses force local regularity).

Suppose ϕ\phi is smooth with constant ambient rank q>0q>0 near θ0\theta_{0}. Under (O), its common arbitrary KK agrees on the whole local represented image near z0=ϕ⁡(θ0)z_{0}=\phi(\theta_{0}) with a smooth function, admitting a smooth extension KlocK_{\rm loc} to a target neighborhood. If ϕ\phi is analytic the section and local extension can be analytic. No Lie-rank assumption is needed.

Proof. See Appendix A.3.

Lemma 2.6 (Local descent and global represented extension).

Let LL be a local plaque on which ϕ\phi has constant rank qq. If D⁡(M|L)D(M|_{L}) annihilates ker⁡D⁡(ϕ|L)\ker D(\phi|_{L}) throughout a neighborhood of θ0\theta_{0} in LL, then M=k∘ϕM=k\circ\phi on a smaller plaque neighborhood for a smooth local represented kk. If LL is the exact local level of common laws, this gives (I) after shrinking the parameter box.

Proof. See Appendix A.4.

3 Complete classification for wide two-factor representations

We identify matrix spaces with Euclidean spaces using the Frobenius inner product. Put

N=n+m,J=diag⁡(In,−Im),F=[UV],C=F​F⊤=[AZZ⊤B],S=F⊤​J​F.N=n+m,\qquad J=\diag(I_{n},-I_{m}),\qquad F=\begin{bmatrix}U\\ V\end{bmatrix},\qquad C=FF^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}A&Z\\ Z^{\top}&B\end{bmatrix},\qquad S=F^{\top}JF.

Here U∈ℝn×rU\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, V∈ℝm×rV\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}, and ϕ⁡(F)=Z=U​V⊤\phi(F)=Z=UV^{\top}. Direct differentiation gives

D​ϕ​(F)​[δ​U,δ​V]=δ​U​V⊤+U​δ​V⊤,D​ϕ​(F)⊤​G=[G​VG⊤​U].D\phi(F)[\delta U,\delta V]=\delta UV^{\top}+U\delta V^{\top},\qquad D\phi(F)^{\top}G=\begin{bmatrix}GV\\ G^{\top}U\end{bmatrix}.

Consequently the full represented mobility is the linear operator

MF​[G]=A​G+G​B,A=U​U⊤,B=V​V⊤.M_{F}[G]=AG+GB,\qquad A=UU^{\top},\quad B=VV^{\top}. (3)

For G∈ℝn×mG\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}, write

HG=[0GG⊤0],XG​(F)=−HG​F.H_{G}=\begin{bmatrix}0&G\\ G^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad X_{G}(F)=-H_{G}F.

These are the parameter gradient fields of the linear represented losses. An arbitrary represented loss f∈C2​(ℝn×m,ℝ)f\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n\times m},\mathbb{R}) gives

F˙=−Hgrad⁡f⁡(Z)​F.\dot{F}=-H_{\grad f(Z)}F. (4)

For clarity, property (O) at F0F_{0} means that one map K:ℝn×m→ℝ(n​m)×(n​m)K:\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\to\mathbb{R}^{(nm)\times(nm)}, independent of ff, equals the entire MFM_{F} along every such autonomous flow from F0F_{0}, until first exit from one common parameter neighborhood. No regularity of KK is assumed. Property (I) means that a finite family of common local C1C^{1} conservation laws hh, together with a globally C1C^{1} represented map K¯\overline{K}, gives MF=K¯​(ϕ​(F))M_{F}=\overline{K}(\phi(F)) on the exact local level h⁡(F)=h⁡(F0)h(F)=h(F_{0}). The conservation laws need only be defined on a parameter neighborhood. Conservation and the chain rule show that (I) implies (O).

The gradient Lie algebra and the factor-orbit dimensions used below are prior ingredients of the conservation-law framework of Marcotte, Gribonval, and Peyré [2], Propositions H.3 and H.5. We include their elementary linear-algebra derivations to make the present argument complete. Likewise the positive scalar-balanced square-root dynamics are known [1, 3]; the classification below concerns their initialization conditions.

Theorem 3.1 (Wide initialization classification).

Assume n,m≥1n,m\geq 1, r>max⁡(n,m)r>\max(n,m), and rank⁡U0=n\rank U_{0}=n, rank⁡V0=m\rank V_{0}=m. Set L0=max⁡(n,m)L_{0}=\max(n,m), s=rank⁡F0s=\rank F_{0}, and C0=F0​F0⊤C_{0}=F_{0}F_{0}^{\top}. Properties (O) and (I), with the latter interpreted in the original width-rr parameter space, are equivalent to the union of the following disjoint cases:

s=L0,C0​J​C0=λ​C0for some ​λ∈ℝ;\displaystyle s=L_{0},\qquad C_{0}JC_{0}=\lambda C_{0}\quad\hbox{for some }\lambda\in\mathbb{R}; (5)
s=N,spec(JC0)={a with multiplicity n,−b with multiplicity m},a,b>0.\displaystyle s=N,\qquad\operatorname{spec}(JC_{0})=\{a\text{ with multiplicity }n,\,-b\text{ with multiplicity }m\},\quad a,b>0. (6)

In (5), n>mn>m forces λ>0\lambda>0, m>nm>n forces λ<0\lambda<0, and n=mn=m permits any λ\lambda. There are no positive cases with L0<s<NL_{0}<s<N. The mobility in either positive case is

Kσ​(Z)​[G]=σ2​In+Z​Z⊤​G+G​σ2​Im+Z⊤​Z,K_{\sigma}(Z)[G]=\sqrt{\sigma^{2}I_{n}+ZZ^{\top}}\,G+G\sqrt{\sigma^{2}I_{m}+Z^{\top}Z}, (7)

where σ=|λ|/2\sigma=|\lambda|/2 in (5) and σ=(a+b)/2\sigma=(a+b)/2 in (6). For σ=0\sigma=0, the formula is used on an invertible represented neighborhood and extended smoothly by a cutoff.

3.1 Factor orbits and the ordinary-closure obstruction

Lemma 3.2 (Boost algebra and factor-orbit dimension).

The fields XGX_{G} generate the left action of

𝔬⁡(n,m)={T∈ℝN×N:T⊤​J+J​T=0}.\mathfrak{o}(n,m)=\{T\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}:T^{\top}J+JT=0\}.

At a factor matrix of rank ss, its local orbit has dimension

dF=(N2)−(N−s2)=s⁡(2​N−s−1)2.d_{F}=\binom{N}{2}-\binom{N-s}{2}=\frac{s(2N-s-1)}{2}. (8)

This formula does not require JJ restricted to im⁡F\operatorname{im}F to be nondegenerate. Every common C1C^{1} conservation law is constant on the connected local orbit.

Proof. See Appendix B.1.

Lemma 3.3 (A necessary Gram-orbit dimension bound).

If F0≠0F_{0}\neq 0 satisfies (O), then the congruence orbit of C0=F0​F0⊤C_{0}=F_{0}F_{0}^{\top} under the JJ-orthogonal group has dimension dC≤n​md_{C}\leq nm. The same bound follows from (I), for arbitrary finite families of common C1C^{1} conservation laws.

Proof. See Appendix B.2.

3.5 The matching known positive dynamics

Proposition 3.10 (Exact narrow scalar-balanced realization).

For σ>0\sigma>0 and every Z∈ℝn×mZ\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}, the operator (7) is realized by width min⁡(n,m)\min(n,m) factors with scalar hidden imbalance. This includes rank-deficient ZZ. For σ=0\sigma=0 and square invertible ZZ, a balanced realization exists locally as well. Thus the positive cases in Theorem 3.1 do not provide new represented continuous-time trajectories.

Proof. See Appendix B.10.

Corollary 3.11 (Generic continuously sampled wide factors).

Let r>max⁡(n,m)r>\max(n,m). For any jointly absolutely continuous initialization law on the full factor space, properties (O) and (I) have probability zero if (n,m)≠(1,1)(n,m)\neq(1,1). For the scalar pair they have probability one. No independence of the factor entries is required.

Proof. See Appendix B.11.

Remark 3.12.

The corollary is a direct classification consequence. It concerns exact entire-mobility closure, with an unrestricted universal loss-testing class. It gives no quantitative approximate closure, learning-performance, stochastic, or discrete-time claim. Neither the classification nor its proof covers every individually rank-deficient block initialization.

4 From initialized trajectory tests to a local metric

We use the ordinary closure and local metric properties in Definitions 2.1 and 2.2. Throughout this section the parameter metric is the original Euclidean metric. Write

M=D​ϕ​D​ϕ𝖳,ℋ=image⁡D​ϕ𝖳,ℰ=Lie⁡{grad⁡ϕi:1≤i≤d}.M=D\phi D\phi^{\mathsf{T}},\qquad\mathcal{H}=\operatorname{image}D\phi^{\mathsf{T}},\qquad\mathcal{E}=\operatorname{Lie}\{\grad\phi_{i}:1\leq i\leq d\}.

Here the last expression denotes the pointwise distribution of the generated Lie algebra. Unless stated otherwise, its rank pp and the rank qq of D​ϕD\phi are constant on an ambient open neighborhood of the initialization θ0\theta_{0}. All subsequent shrinkages are inside the common neighborhood in the ordinary closure hypothesis. Frobenius, the constant-rank theorem, smooth dependence of ODE solutions, and tubular coordinates are used in their classical local forms.

Lemma 4.1 (The regular initial plaque).

There is a smooth Frobenius product box with finitely many smooth common conservation laws hh, whose initial level is one connected pp-dimensional plaque LL tangent to ℰ\mathcal{E}. If ϕ\phi is real analytic, this box, LL, and hh can be chosen real analytic. On LL, D⁡(ϕ|L)D(\phi|_{L}) has constant rank qq.

Proof. See Appendix C.1.

Theorem 4.2 (Regular analytic and specified smooth regimes).

For a real-analytic representation with the two constant ambient ranks, ordinary closure is equivalent to a local invariant-level metric. The same equivalence holds for a smooth representation when q≥3q\geq 3, when q≤1q\leq 1, or when q=2q=2 and p≤3p\leq 3. The conservation laws and the global represented extension in the conclusion can be smooth.

4.1 The analytic case and the exact descent

Proof of Theorem 4.2 in the analytic case. See Appendix C.2.

4.2 Smooth horizontal paths in represented rank at least three

Lemma 4.3 (An elementary embedded-arc approximation).

Let q≥3q\geq 3 and let w:[0,T]→ℝqw:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^{q}, T>0T>0, be smooth, with compact image in an open coordinate set. There are vectors aj→0a_{j}\to 0 for which wj​(t)=w⁡(t)+t​ajw_{j}(t)=w(t)+ta_{j} are regular embedded smooth arcs, remain in the same coordinate set, have wj​(0)=w​(0)w_{j}(0)=w(0), and converge to ww in C1C^{1}. Their other endpoints need only converge.

Proof. See Appendix C.3.

Lemma 4.4 (Closure on a smooth horizontal path).

Assume ordinary closure, the constant representation rank, and q≥3q\geq 3. On a sufficiently small parameter neighborhood, every smooth path from θ0\theta_{0} tangent to ℋ\mathcal{H} satisfies M=Kloc∘ϕM=K_{\mathrm{loc}}\circ\phi, where KlocK_{\mathrm{loc}} is the forced smooth representative of Lemma 2.5.

Proof. See Appendix C.4.

Lemma 4.5 (Local finite-word accessibility).

On the regular plaque LL, every point of a sufficiently small neighborhood of θ0\theta_{0} is the endpoint of a finite horizontal flow word lying in a prescribed slightly larger plaque neighborhood. Such words admit smooth horizontal time reparametrizations with the same endpoints.

Proof. See Appendix C.5.

Proof of Theorem 4.2 for q≥3q\geq 3 and the elementary low-rank cases. See Appendix C.6.

4.3 The rank-two, three-dimensional-leaf case

Lemma 4.6 (A finite horizontal curvature jet).

Suppose q=2,p=3q=2,p=3. On LL, choose coordinates (u,v,η)(u,v,\eta) with (u,v)=π(u,v)=\pi represented coordinates and θ0=(0,0,0)\theta_{0}=(0,0,0). Write its horizontal lifts as

H1=∂u+A∂η,H2=∂v+B∂η,[H1,H2]=c∂η.H_{1}=\partial_{u}+A\partial_{\eta},\qquad H_{2}=\partial_{v}+B\partial_{\eta},\qquad[H_{1},H_{2}]=c\partial_{\eta}.

Some finite ordered horizontal derivative of cc is nonzero at θ0\theta_{0}. If mm is the least such order, the leading word tensor is symmetric and the homogeneous polynomial Pm​(e)=Hem​c​(θ0)P_{m}(e)=H_{e}^{m}c(\theta_{0}), He=e1​H1+e2​H2H_{e}=e_{1}H_{1}+e_{2}H_{2}, is not identically zero. Lemma 4.7 (Four rectangle families and a common fiber interval).

Under the preceding hypotheses there are two independent unit base directions and their negatives, and one fixed small ε>0\varepsilon>0, such that the signed rectangle loops in any of these four directions have horizontal endpoints covering one common open interval about θ0\theta_{0} in the initial one-dimensional fiber.

with δ\delta sufficiently small.

4.4 All-order and Euclidean necessary conditions

Proposition 4.9 (All-order flatness at the initial plaque).

Under smooth constant ambient ranks and ordinary closure, take Kloc=0K_{\mathrm{loc}}=0 when q=0q=0 and otherwise use the smooth representative from Lemma 2.5. Set R=M−Kloc∘ϕR=M-K_{\mathrm{loc}}\circ\phi. Every finite plaque-coordinate derivative of R|LR|_{L} at θ0\theta_{0} vanishes.

Suppose q=2q=2. Let u=a⋅ϕ+c0u=a\cdot\phi+c_{0} and v=b⋅ϕv=b\cdot\phi be constant output-linear combinations with independent gradients X=grad⁡uX=\grad u, Y=grad⁡vY=\grad v on the chosen neighborhood. Remark 4.11.

The general smooth case q=2,p≥4q=2,p\geq 4 is not settled here. Proposition 4.9 makes a counterexample’s actual mobility discrepancy flat to every order at the initialization, but does not rule out a nonzero smooth flat discrepancy. A planar non-density observation or an arbitrary connection is not by itself a Euclidean representation satisfying the universal ordinary premise. None of these results asserts a new positive optimizer, discrete dynamics, or an implication from a single observed loss.

5 Exact autonomous-loss exclusion controls

The following constructions illustrate the logical strength of the ordinary premise. They are algebraic witnesses, not experiments or separate novelty claims. They do not refute the bridge theorem, because they fail its ordinary closure assumption.

Proposition 5.1 (Arbitrarily delayed brackets and a two-loss witness).

For each integer k≥2k\geq 2, let ϕk​(x,y,z)=(x,y+xk​z)\phi_{k}(x,y,z)=(x,y+x^{k}z). Its representation rank is two and its gradient Lie rank is three everywhere. At the origin all iterated brackets of lengths two through kk vanish, while a bracket of length k+1k+1 supplies the third direction. The first differential mobility test passes at the origin, yet ordinary closure fails there, as witnessed by two global smooth autonomous losses.

Proof. See Appendix D.1.

Proposition 5.2 (A rank-four affine-output exclusion).

For ϕ⁡(x,y,z,w)=(x,y+x​z+z​w)\phi(x,y,z,w)=(x,y+xz+zw), q=2q=2 and p=4p=4 everywhere, and ordinary closure fails at every initialization.

Proof. See Appendix D.2.

6 What restricted loss families test

The arbitrary-loss quantifier in property (O) is substantive. For a family ℱ\mathcal{F} of global output losses, write (O)ℱ\textup{(O)}_{\mathcal{F}} for the same property with only f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} tested: one parameter neighborhood UU and one entire matrix map K:ℝd→ℝd×dK:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, independent of ff, must satisfy

M⁡(θf​(t))=K⁡(ϕ⁡(θf​(t)))M(\theta_{f}(t))=K(\phi(\theta_{f}(t)))

on every forward local solution interval before exit from UU, from the same fixed initialization. The matrix KK is initially arbitrary. In particular the equality concerns the entire mobility, rather than only its product with the tested loss gradient. Property (O) restricts to every smaller family, but its necessity conclusions cannot be transferred in the opposite direction without proof. The following supporting results make this distinction explicit.

Proposition 6.1 (Linear tests at a submersion).

Suppose ϕ\phi is smooth and D​ϕ​(θ0)D\phi(\theta_{0}) has full row rank dd. Then (O)ℱlin\textup{(O)}_{\mathcal{F}_{\rm lin}} holds for ℱlin={z↦gT​z:g∈ℝd}\mathcal{F}_{\rm lin}=\{z\mapsto g^{T}z:g\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\}. A common KK can be chosen globally smooth after shrinking the parameter neighborhood. This holds for all gg, without a common bound on its norm.

Proof. See Appendix E.1.

For k≥2k\geq 2, consider

ϕk(x,y,z)=(x,y+xkz),X=∂x,Y=(kxk−1z,1,xk).\phi_{k}(x,y,z)=(x,y+x^{k}z),\qquad X=\partial_{x},\quad Y=(kx^{k-1}z,1,x^{k}).

hy+xk​hz=0h_{y}+x^{k}h_{z}=0

At fixed output (a,0)(a,0) the parameter states (a,−ak​z,z)(a,-a^{k}z,z) have M12=k​ak−1​zM_{12}=ka^{k-1}z, which varies for arbitrarily small nonzero aa and zz. Remark 6.5 (Scope and a positive control).

The readout in Corollary 6.4 is a fixed change of represented features, not a change in the Euclidean parameter metric. It does not establish identity-Hessian failure on the original untransformed ϕk\phi_{k}, a collision at equal times for the same fixed Hessian, or a failure for one fixed target. Choosing γ=1/2\gamma=1/2 fixes Hessian condition number three. The corresponding projection representation ψ0=W⁡(x,y)\psi_{0}=W(x,y) has constant mobility HH, and therefore admits closure for every loss. Linear tests also pass for ψk\psi_{k} by Proposition 6.1. These statements distinguish the loss families; they do not constitute a new optimizer, training gain or general quadratic-family classification.

Proposition 6.6 (Quadratic tests force section regularity).

Suppose ϕ\phi is smooth and has constant ambient rank q>0q>0 on a neighborhood of θ0\theta_{0}. Set z0=ϕ⁡(θ0)z_{0}=\phi(\theta_{0}) and test only

fb​(z)=12​‖z−z0‖22+bT​(z−z0),b∈ℝd.f_{b}(z)=\tfrac{1}{2}\|z-z_{0}\|_{2}^{2}+b^{T}(z-z_{0}),\qquad b\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

If (O){fb:b∈ℝd}\textup{(O)}_{\{f_{b}:b\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\}} holds, then its arbitrary common KK agrees on a local represented image with a smooth representative. That representative has a local ambient extension, and after shrinking the image it has a global smooth extension. If ϕ\phi is analytic, the representative on the image and its local extension can be analytic. This is an image-section conclusion, not an invariant-level factorization.

Proof. See Appendix E.4.

Proposition 6.6 identifies KK on an actual endpoint section. It says nothing by itself about other parameter points of the same represented fiber. Proposition 6.1 and Remark 6.2 explain why section regularity alone cannot substitute for the full arbitrary-loss necessity arguments. The supporting results here remove a loss-family limitation of the explicit negative control while retaining that distinction. They imply no numerical value of a∗a_{*}, empirical convergence order, universal quadratic-family converse, or learning-performance claim.

7 Related Work

Intrinsic dynamics and initialized tests.

Marcotte, Peyré, and Gribonval [1] introduce the ordinary intrinsic-dynamic and invariant-metric notions used here, together with a stronger definition for piecewise 𝒞2\mathcal{C}^{2} autonomous losses. Their Theorem 3.8 gives a positive relaxed-balance branch. Their Theorem 3.9 assumes full-rank factors and hidden width at most max⁡(n,m)\max(n,m), and excludes their strong intrinsic dynamic property outside relaxed balance. Proposition 3.10 already resolves n=m=1n=m=1 at arbitrary width. Our wide classification addresses ordinary closure with individually full-row factors; its scalar subcase is inherited. Their Theorem 2.14 starts from a differentiable invariant-level metric and Theorem 2.17 from recoverability. The converse here starts from an unrestricted KK and fixed-start autonomous tests, including specified cases with Lie rank larger than representation rank.

The conservation-law framework of Marcotte, Gribonval, and Peyré [2], Theorem 3.3 and Propositions H.3/H.5, supplies the Lie distribution, the count of independent common laws, and matrix factor-orbit ingredients. Their Proposition 3.7 concerns recovery from invariants and representation. The additional necessity step here passes from actual autonomous endpoint patches to mobility constraints on Gram fibers. A factor-orbit dimension count alone does not supply that step.

Known positive matrix flows and larger closed states.

Dominé et al. [3], Theorem 5.2 and Appendix C.2.1, recover the factors up to hidden orthogonal transformations, and thereby determine the two mobility Gram blocks, under their λ\lambda-balanced and full-rank-product assumptions, giving the square-root structure. Bah et al. [4], Lemma 2 and Propositions 10–11, give the balanced product flow and its Riemannian interpretation on fixed-rank matrix manifolds. These are positive reduction results. The initialization exclusion and original ambient invariant-level arguments in Theorem 3.1 answer a different necessity question. Proposition 3.10 explicitly matches our positive flows to a known narrow family.

Zhang and Peyré [5], Proposition 2.1, close the flow on the full weight covariance, retaining the hidden Gram blocks. The state here is only Z=U​V⊤Z=UV^{\top}. Importantly, their Proposition E.2 also gives predictor-only square-root closure on the hyperbolically isotropic leaf C​J​C=α2​JCJC=\alpha^{2}J after the appropriate width normalization; this is the a=ba=b part of our full-rank positive branch. For the unequal pair, the fixed shift D=C−(a−b)​J/2D=C-(a-b)J/2 satisfies D​J​D=((a+b)/2)2​JDJD=((a+b)/2)^{2}J and has the same covariance flow because HG​J+J​HG=0H_{G}J+JH_{G}=0. Thus this positive reduction remains a known-family consequence. Their Remark E.3 shows that conserved spectral values generally do not determine predictor velocity. That two-state example does not itself establish ordinary failure from one fixed initialization. We make no novelty claim for covariance closure or the positive square-root formula, and do not infer a global priority claim from this comparison.

Geometric criteria and mirror flows.

Li et al. [6], Theorem 4.9, obtain mirror flow from a regular commuting parametrization under their flow-domain assumptions. Theorem 4.10 gives a necessary Lie-bracket condition when a mirror representation works for all initializations and time-dependent losses. Mirror flow requires an integrable inverse-Hessian metric, whereas properties (O) and (I) allow general mobility. Our initialized autonomous-loss premise and invariant-level conclusion therefore have different quantifiers and targets. Horstmeyer and Atay [7], Proposition 1 and Theorem 4, characterize exact lumpability by all-state projectability and invariance of the vertical distribution under Lie differentiation. Their criterion applies to a fixed vector field on smooth manifolds with the stated submersion/fiber hypotheses. Applying it backwards here would first require proving nearby-fiber consistency from initialized tests; this is precisely the extra implication we study.

Achour, Kohn, and Rauhut [8], Theorem 4 and Corollary 6 in the April 2026 revision, show that for one-dimensional linear convolutional networks with the specified strides larger than one, fixed norm-difference invariants determine the NTK on the smooth neuromanifold, with finite fibers. Their broader work also treats higher-dimensional convolutions. The finite-fiber recovery geometry differs from the matrix-factorization fibers and p>qp>q regimes considered here. We do not extend the matrix classification to convolutional architectures.

Optimization and implicit bias.

Saxe et al. [9] provide exact deep-linear learning solutions for structured settings. Arora et al. [10] interpret depth-induced preconditioning; Gunasekar et al. [11] and Arora et al. [12] study implicit regularization in matrix factorization. These motivate examining represented dynamics, but a convergence or bias result under one loss is not an all-loss mobility classification. Min et al. [13] bound convergence using imbalance and product singular values. Nordio [14] studies training-set dynamics with fixed readout and quadratic loss, retaining a hierarchy of Gram operators at depth. Castin et al. [15] use balancing to change LoRA conditioning. Our results concern continuous Euclidean parameter gradient flow and claim neither their discrete-time guarantees nor an improvement in learning performance.

8 Discussion and Limitations

Theorem 3.1 determines when the prediction matrix can serve as a complete mobility state for every autonomous loss from one fixed initialization. In the nonscalar wide model, its generic nonclosure corollary rules out that exact description under absolutely continuous initialization. It leaves open approximate closure, loss-specific reductions, and dynamics on larger states such as a full covariance.

The factors must be individually full row rank and r>max⁡(n,m)r>\max(n,m). Individually deficient initializations are not classified. The general bridge requires representation and gradient-Lie ranks constant on an ambient open neighborhood; singular width reduction does not transfer that hypothesis. The smooth case q=2,p≥4q=2,p\geq 4 remains unresolved. All-order flatness alone cannot replace equality of a smooth function on a neighborhood. The fixed-Hessian quadratic witness is theoretical: no numerical a∗a_{*}, quadratic grid, or empirical convergence order is asserted. The historical engineered-loss check in Appendix G is a different test. Continuous-time mobility equality does not imply equality of finite-step updates.

A.1 Proof of Lemma 2.3

Proof.

Tangential compatibility and the prescribed normal derivatives give grad⁡floc​(γ⁡(t))=g⁡(t)\grad f_{\rm loc}(\gamma(t))=g(t). For d=1d=1 there are no normal variables. Multiply by a smooth cutoff supported inside the extended tube and identically one near the original compact arc, and extend by zero to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. This is one global smooth loss. Uniqueness for its locally Lipschitz parameter ODE identifies the prescribed path with the actual autonomous trajectory. The slight extension prevents endpoint regularity problems. The scalar compatibility also gives A′=−gT​M​g=−‖θ˙‖2A^{\prime}=-g^{T}Mg=-\|\dot{\theta}\|^{2} along the curve; we have not prescribed inconsistent values around a projected loop. ∎

A.2 Proof of Lemma 2.4

Proof.

Choose gcg_{c} with gcT​M​(θ0)​gc>0g_{c}^{T}M(\theta_{0})g_{c}>0. On a smaller state box and a bounded convex open ball BB about gcg_{c}, continuity gives gcT​M​(θ)​g≥c>0g_{c}^{T}M(\theta)g\geq c>0 for all g∈Bg\in B. Thus along these controls

dd​t​⟨gc,ϕ⁡(θ⁡(t))⟩=−gcT​M​(θ⁡(t))​g​(t)≤−c.\frac{d}{dt}\langle g_{c},\phi(\theta(t))\rangle=-g_{c}^{T}M(\theta(t))g(t)\leq-c.

Smooth controlled projected paths are regular and embedded. A compact state box and uniform speed bound give a short horizon ε\varepsilon keeping every finite word of controls in BB with total duration less than ε\varepsilon inside the chosen neighborhood. The bound depends on total time, not the number of switches. Differences of members of BB span all controls, so their Lie values still span T​LTL.

Let QQ be the maximum differential rank of all positive-duration word endpoint maps from θ0\theta_{0} with total time less than ε\varepsilon. Integer boundedness ensures a word and a strictly positive duration vector attain QQ. On a small duration patch its rank is constantly QQ, giving an embedded local image PP. Append a short positive segment of any fixed YgY_{g}, g∈Bg\in B. The augmented endpoint map has rank at most QQ by maximality. Its (Q+1)(Q+1)-minors remain zero as the appended duration decreases to zero, while the original QQ-minor persists. The appended derivative is YgY_{g}, so YgY_{g} is tangent to PP throughout a local patch. Brackets of tangent fields are tangent. The Lie spanning hypothesis forces Q≥dimLQ\geq\dim L, hence equality. This gives a word endpoint image with nonempty interior in LL, without claiming that it contains θ0\theta_{0} or arbitrary return fibers.

Insert between successive fixed controls smooth flat-ended convex ramps of one fixed duration δ\delta, keeping the plateau durations as parameters. On a compact neighborhood, uniform field and state-Jacobian bounds imply for each ramp map TδT_{\delta}

‖Tδ−I‖≤C​δ,‖D​Tδ−I‖≤eC​δ−1.\|T_{\delta}-I\|\leq C\delta,\qquad\|DT_{\delta}-I\|\leq e^{C\delta}-1.

These follow from the flow integral and variational equations; no bound on the control’s time derivatives is needed. Finite composition yields convergence of the endpoint maps in state and duration derivatives. A full-rank minor therefore persists for one sufficiently small positive δ\delta, with the extra times within the strict horizon margin. The smoothed family itself, not merely its limit, has an LL-open endpoint image. The clock inequality still holds and each control is constant near the outer endpoints, so slight extensions remain embedded. Lemma 2.3 realizes each by one global autonomous smooth loss. The common KK in (O) then gives the identity on the endpoint patch. No derivative or limit of an unrestricted KK has been used. ∎

A.4 Proof of Lemma 2.6

Proof.

In a constant-rank product chart on LL, the representation depends only on qq coordinates and the assumed derivative identity makes MM independent of the other coordinates. Restrict to a product with connected fibers to factor MM through the local embedded image. Extend normally in target coordinates to an open W∋z0W\ni z_{0}, obtaining KlocK_{\rm loc}. This gives the actual local-level identity and global smooth target extension. The argument is local and does not identify disconnected global fibers. The analytic local descent follows in analytic charts; the final cutoff is smooth. ∎

B.1 Proof of Lemma 3.2

Proof.

The local orbit statement therefore makes it constant on the connected local orbit. Alternatively one may use finite boost products and their commutator limits, passing invariance through continuity. B.11 Proof of Corollary 3.11

Proof.

Separate maximal row ranks and maximal joint rank hold almost surely: their failures lie in zero sets of nonzero minor polynomials. If r<Nr<N, the almost-sure joint rank is rr, strictly between L0L_{0} and NN, so Theorem 3.1 excludes closure. If r≥Nr\geq N, the almost-sure joint rank is NN. For (n,m)≠(1,1)(n,m)\neq(1,1), the positive spectral case forces a repeated eigenvalue of J​F​F⊤JFF^{\top}. The discriminant

P⁡(F)=disc⁡dett⁡(t​IN−J​F​F⊤)P(F)=\operatorname{disc}_{t}\det(tI_{N}-JFF^{\top})

is a polynomial in the factor entries and must vanish there. It is not identically zero: at F=[diag⁡(1,…,N),0]F=[\diag(1,\ldots,N),0] its signed diagonal eigenvalues are all distinct. The zero set of a nonzero real polynomial has Lebesgue measure zero, and hence probability zero under every such law. For n=m=1n=m=1, the two factor rows are nonzero almost surely. Joint rank one automatically gives C​J​C=λ​CCJC=\lambda C; joint rank two automatically gives one positive and one negative signed spectral value. The theorem then gives closure, in agreement with the known scalar case [1, Proposition 3.10]. ∎

Appendix C Proofs of the geometric characterization

C.1 Proof of Lemma 4.1

Proof.

Select finitely many bracket fields V1,…,VpV_{1},\ldots,V_{p} independent at θ0\theta_{0}. A nonzero frame minor stays nonzero on a smaller neighborhood; constant rank makes these fields a frame for ℰ\mathcal{E} there. Their brackets belong pointwise to ℰ\mathcal{E}, and their frame coefficients are smooth, or analytic in the analytic case, by inversion of the fixed frame minor. Leibniz’s rule then makes this subbundle involutive. The corresponding smooth or analytic Frobenius theorem supplies coordinates (x,h)(x,h) in a product box, with ℰ=ker⁡D​h\mathcal{E}=\ker Dh. The components of hh annihilate every grad⁡ϕi\grad\phi_{i}, so they are common conservation laws. The set h=h⁡(θ0)h=h(\theta_{0}) in this box is a single connected plaque. If p=Dp=D, one may take hh constant.

Because ℋ⊂ℰ=T​L\mathcal{H}\subset\mathcal{E}=TL, restriction of D​ϕD\phi to T​LTL has image containing

image⁡(D​ϕ​D​ϕ𝖳)=image⁡D​ϕ.\operatorname{image}(D\phi D\phi^{\mathsf{T}})=\operatorname{image}D\phi.

The reverse containment is automatic. Thus the restriction has the same rank qq. No full-output-rank assumption is involved. ∎

C.5 Proof of Lemma 4.5

Proof.

Use positive durations and the finite symmetric field family {grad⁡ϕi,−grad⁡ϕi}\{\grad\phi_{i},-\grad\phi_{i}\}. A uniform speed bound on a compact chart gives a sufficiently short total horizon for all words under consideration. Maximize the differential rank of their endpoint maps over all finite words and strictly positive duration vectors. The maximum QQ is attained, since ranks are integers bounded by pp. Around a maximizing vector, a nonzero QQ-minor persists and no higher rank is possible. The constant-rank theorem gives an embedded image patch PP of dimension QQ with a strict remaining horizon margin.

Append any one of the allowed fields for an additional positive duration. Maximality bounds the augmented rank by QQ. Taking that duration to zero makes its extra derivative tangent to PP; the original QQ-minor still persists. Thus all the generators, and hence their brackets, are tangent to PP. Their Lie rank is pp, so Q=pQ=p and PP is open in LL.

Let the fixed maximizing word end at θ∗\theta_{*}. Its inverse word is a local diffeomorphism sending θ∗\theta_{*} to θ0\theta_{0} and a smaller open patch PP to a neighborhood of θ0\theta_{0} in LL. Every point of that neighborhood is obtained by a nearby forward word followed by this fixed inverse word. Finite-path continuous dependence ensures that all these paths stay in the larger chart after shrinking PP. This uses control words only as horizontal paths; it does not call their concatenation a single autonomous loss.

For each segment, replace its time parameter by a smooth increasing function with the same endpoints and all derivatives zero at both ends. The resulting joined path is smooth and horizontal, including at the joins, and has exactly the same image and endpoint. ∎

C.6 Proof of Theorem 4.2 for q≥3q\geq 3 and the elementary low-rank cases

Proof of Theorem 4.2 for q≥3q\geq 3 and the elementary low-rank cases.

For q≥3q\geq 3, Lemmas 4.4 and 4.5 give the mobility identity on an entire neighborhood of θ0\theta_{0} in its initial plaque. Shrink the original Frobenius product box so its actual initial level lies there. A target cutoff as in the analytic proof makes KlocK_{\mathrm{loc}} globally smooth and proves the metric property.

If q=0q=0, the stationary argument already applies. If q=1q=1, the regular horizontal line bundle is involutive, so p=1p=1. More generally, whenever p=qp=q, ϕ\phi is locally injective on the initial plaque by the constant-rank theorem. A local section factors MM smoothly through its represented image, and target extension and cutoff give the metric property without assuming ordinary closure. These are the classical local recoverability cases. It remains to prove the smooth q=2,p=3q=2,p=3 case. ∎

C.11 Proof of Proposition 4.9

Proof.

The stationary case is immediate. Otherwise fix one open clock ball BB and a state box inside the domain of KlocK_{\mathrm{loc}}. For any fixed finite sequence g1,…,gk∈Bg_{1},\ldots,g_{k}\in B, let E⁡(t)E(t) be the flow-word endpoint at durations t1,…,tkt_{1},\ldots,t_{k}. All sufficiently small positive duration vectors have a strict represented clock. Smooth control ramps and the compatible autonomous jet construction give genuine single-global-loss endpoints tending to E⁡(t)E(t). The smooth representative permits the limit, so R⁡(E⁡(t))=0R(E(t))=0 throughout the positive open duration orthant near zero.

The finite endpoint map extends smoothly to a full neighborhood of zero durations. Every mixed derivative of R∘ER\circ E on the positive orthant is zero and remains zero at its corner by continuity. Differentiating once in each duration yields

Yg1⋯YgkR(θ0)=0,Yg=−Dϕ𝖳g,Y_{g_{1}}\cdots Y_{g_{k}}R(\theta_{0})=0,\qquad Y_{g}=-D\phi^{\mathsf{T}}g,

with the naming order fixed by pullback convention; every sequence order is available. The zero-order identity follows at the initial time. Negative durations are used only to define derivatives of a smooth map, not as assumed test trajectories.

For each fixed kk the displayed evaluation is multilinear in its constant controls. Vanishing on BkB^{k} extends it to all controls, and therefore to all ordered coordinate-gradient words. Every bracket field is a finite signed combination of such differential operator words, and products of bracket fields retain this property. Choose a finite local bracket frame V1,…,VpV_{1},\ldots,V_{p} for ℰ\mathcal{E}. All its ordered products annihilate RR at θ0\theta_{0}. Each plaque-coordinate vector field is a smooth linear combination of this frame. Repeated Leibniz expansion of any coordinate derivative consequently consists of smooth coefficients times ordered frame derivatives of RR, all zero at θ0\theta_{0}. This proves flatness in every plaque chart. The argument does not identify a smooth flat function with zero on a neighborhood. ∎

C.12 Proof of Proposition 4.10

Proof.

Since q=2q=2, X,YX,Y smoothly frame ℋ\mathcal{H}. Put λ=⟨X,Y⟩=a𝖳​M​b\lambda=\langle X,Y\rangle=a^{\mathsf{T}}Mb. Euclidean differentiation gives the exact identity

Its gradient is therefore orthogonal to ℰ∩ker⁡D​ϕ\mathcal{E}\cap\ker D\phi. Because it also lies in ℰ\mathcal{E}, it belongs to ℋ\mathcal{H}, the orthogonal complement of that vertical subspace inside ℰ\mathcal{E}. The identity above then makes [X,Y][X,Y] horizontal on OO.

Appendix F Finite checks and reproducibility

The universal statements above rest on the included proofs. Existing exact algebraic checks are finite implementation evidence and were not rerun to produce this manuscript. The latest boundary validation used rational arithmetic on 39 fixtures: 24 effective scalar-imbalance and 15 nonscalar cases, including four zero-scalar cases. It checked 259 hidden-rotation and tangent identities and reported zero mismatches. These were bounded algebraic checks, not model training. These finite checks neither prove the universal classification nor establish task accuracy, statistical uncertainty, approximate-closure error or a practical speedup.

The local provenance audit preserves the available inputs, proof versions, automated review records, primary source texts, and their hashes. Complete local source custody is distinguished from selected theorem-and-proof reading. The two closest source versions are arXiv:2508.07370v2 (12 March 2026, ICLR 2026 rendition) and arXiv:2307.00144v2 (10 July 2024 revision of the NeurIPS 2023 work). The following numerical record is copied from a frozen, actually executed experiment. No new scientific run was used to assemble this manuscript. The algebraic and autonomous-loss records answer different finite questions.

Appendix G A finite autonomous-loss implementation check

We executed one deterministic CPU sentinel for the engineered smooth-loss construction in Proposition 5.1. This tests an implementation of a proved mechanism, rather than a learning algorithm. The fixed-Hessian quadratic and ordinary squared-loss extension in this manuscript has not been executed: its numerical a∗a_{*} and any executed quadratic-loss grid remain unknown. The measurements below must not be transferred to that new loss family.

Actual objective and parameter flow.

Set F⁡(u)=ukF(u)=u^{k}, h⁡(u)=u⁡(a−u)h(u)=u(a-u) and D⁡(u)=1+F​(u)2D(u)=1+F(u)^{2}. The implemented global objective was

where

In particular the off-graph term B′​(v−h)B^{\prime}(v-h) was included; substituting the analytic graph for this ODE would not qualify the implementation. The analytic comparison path is (t,h⁡(t)−F⁡(t)​ζ​(t),ζ⁡(t))(t,h(t)-F(t)\zeta(t),\zeta(t)). The comparison loss f1​(u,v)=−uf_{1}(u,v)=-u was also integrated, with analytic path (t,0,0)(t,0,0).

Frozen protocol and discriminating controls.

The twelve witness cases used k∈{2,3,4}k\in\{2,3,4\} and a∈{0.5,0.35,0.25,0.175}a\in\{0.5,0.35,0.25,0.175\}, with ϵ=1\epsilon=1. Four matched controls used F≡0F\equiv 0 at the same aa values; these have p=q=2p=q=2, mobility I2I_{2} and zero gap. We used DOP853 with relative tolerance 2×10−122\times 10^{-12}, absolute tolerance 10−1410^{-14} and 21 stored times per trajectory. Working scalar quadratures used absolute and relative tolerances 10−1310^{-13} and at most 100 subdivisions. Independently, a 50-decimal-digit quadrature evaluated the cancellation-avoiding reference

Δref=−k2​a2​k+11+a2​k∫01tk​(1−t)(1+a2​k​t2​k)3/2dt.\Delta_{\rm ref}=-\frac{k^{2}a^{2k+1}}{\sqrt{1+a^{2k}}}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{t^{k}(1-t)}{(1+a^{2k}t^{2k})^{3/2}}\,dt. (20)

This is a high-precision estimate, not a certified quadrature interval.

Five-point central differences, step 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, differentiated the globally defined scalar loss composed with ϕk\phi_{k} in all three parameter coordinates. Both probes were off graph: (x,y,z)=(0,0.1,0.03)(x,y,z)=(0,0.1,0.03), and x=0.3​ax=0.3a, z=0.02​az=0.02a, v=h⁡(x)+0.05​av=h(x)+0.05a, with y=v−F⁡(x)​zy=v-F(x)z. Each coordinate used tolerance 5×10−8+5×10−6​|gFD|5\times 10^{-8}+5\times 10^{-6}|g_{\rm FD}|. The deliberately incorrect gradient omitting B′​(v−h)B^{\prime}(v-h) had to fail the same tolerance at both probes. Its first-probe discrepancy had to exceed 10−310^{-3}. This matters because the omitted term vanishes on the analytic graph.

Before execution we fixed state error ≤3×10−10\leq 3\times 10^{-10}, represented endpoint error ≤10−10\leq 10^{-10}, nonzero-gap relative error ≤5×10−6\leq 5\times 10^{-6}, and a zero-control gap threshold 10−1210^{-12}. For L=k2​a2​k+1/((k+1)​(k+2))L=k^{2}a^{2k+1}/((k+1)(k+2)), the measured −Δ/L-\Delta/L was compared with [(1+a2​k)−2,(1+a2​k)−1/2][(1+a^{2k})^{-2},(1+a^{2k})^{-1/2}] using slack 5×10−65\times 10^{-6}. Nonfinite outputs could not pass. The first completed failed case or exception would stop the sole attempt; no grid or tolerance was selected after observing results. There are no random seeds or statistical confidence intervals.

Observed results and limits.

All twelve witnesses and four matched controls passed the frozen criteria. The maximum state discrepancy over the 21 stored times was 2.015×10−122.015\times 10^{-12} and represented endpoint discrepancy 1.859×10−131.859\times 10^{-13}; all four F=0F=0 gaps were stored as zero and their identity-mobility checks passed. All 32 off-graph probes passed, with maximum coordinate FD discrepancy 1.043×10−131.043\times 10^{-13}. Every omitted-term mutant was rejected; the minimum across probes of its largest coordinate error was 0.01750.0175. The k=4,a=0.175k=4,a=0.175 ratio band has width 1.3195×10−61.3195\times 10^{-6}, smaller than the allowed slack, and is explicitly tolerance dominated. Passing that band does not demonstrate sharp-band or next-order asymptotic resolution. The integrator tolerances are not global error certificates, and working quadrature error estimates are heuristic.

The historical implementation used 3122 f2f_{2} right-hand-side evaluations and 9057 quadrature calls. No GPU computation or model training was used. Raw trajectories, gradient probes, numerical references, code/input hashes are preserved in the local historical record. The supplied numerical payload can be run independently with the listed dependencies; two original external resource-wrapper files are unavailable, so the historical execution environment and resource measurements are not fully reproducible from this package. The public historical data consist of the exported summary and trajectory CSVs; the original raw probe/reference JSON files and source-custody receipts are not distributed in this package. These finite observations support implementation and mechanism agreement; the exact endpoint equality and universal quantifiers rest on the proofs. They establish no learning improvement, algorithmic speedup, numerical validation of the new quadratic theorem, or general asymptotic law.

Separate pre-submission replay.

A separate pre-submission replay under Python 3.12.14, NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.17.0, and mpmath 1.3.0 passed all 16 cases and 32 off-graph probes, rejecting every omitted-term mutant. It used 3116 f2f_{2} right-hand-side evaluations and 7035 quadrature calls. Source copies, outputs, environment, and comparisons are in anc/audit_replay/. These new results are separate from the historical measurements; they do not reproduce the historical environment or resource wrappers, and do not test the fixed-Hessian quadratic theorem.
